kids.name: Angela Marie Bautista
kids.justification: She would not be ready to let her four-year-old use an AI storyteller without her nearby. If she tried one, she would prefer the inexpensive audio-only app; the dedicated audio-only device costs too much, and she is less interested in options with screens.

kids.name: Sarah Beth Lindstrom
kids.justification: She would choose no AI storyteller for now because she is uncomfortable with a three- to five-year-old using one without supervision. If she tried one, she would prefer E for its low cost and audio-only format, though she would want to control phone use. D avoids screens but costs more; C is cheap but has a screen and phone-access drawbacks; A is costly and adds a screen without addressing her supervision concern.

gaz.name: Jorge Luis Castañeda
gaz.justification: I might try bottled gazpacho once if it was reasonably priced. I like fresh, well-seasoned vegetables, but I usually prefer food that tastes fresh-made, and the price would matter a lot.

gaz.name: Darren Paul Schneider
gaz.justification: He said he’d be very unlikely to buy bottled gazpacho, though he might try a little sample. He usually prefers warm, familiar food, and cold blended vegetables don’t sound especially appealing; he wouldn’t rule it out if it were mild and the price was right.

kids.name: Angela Marie Bautista
kids.justification: D (dedicated audio-only) first — I like that it has no screen so it's gentler at bedtime, is single-purpose (so Mateo won't accidentally open other apps), and can be designed to be kid‑proof and simple. It is pricey compared with an app, I mean it costs as much as a low-end tablet, so we'd have to think about whether it's worth that one-time expense, but for routine use and calmer evenings it's my top pick. E (audio-only app) second — inexpensive (about $10) and we can try it right away on a phone or tablet we already have; good for testing whether Mateo likes independent stories. My worry is accidental access to other apps or notifications unless there's a reliable kid-lock, so it comes second. C (app with images) third — illustrations are nice and Mateo likes pictures, but the screen light and extra stimulation make it less suitable for bedtime and it raises the same worries about device access. A (dedicated audio+images) fourth — safer than an app because it's single-purpose, but the screen makes bedtime harder and it's the same high price as D without the clear advantage for calm routines. B (nothing) last — I value reading aloud myself and the library, and I wouldn't rush to buy tech for stories, but a safe, simple storyteller could be a useful tool when I'm worn out or need a hands-free option. Practical notes: whichever option I pick I'd want clear parental controls, examples of the kinds of stories it tells (to check for age-appropriateness), and a look at durability and any ongoing costs before buying.

kids.name: Sarah Beth Lindstrom
kids.justification: E (app, audio-only) first because it’s the cheapest way to try the idea and gives the bedtime-friendly audio I want without forcing a new device purchase. For us, $10 is something we can try, and if it turns out we hate it or the kids don’t use it, it’s not a big loss. I do worry about kids using a parent phone, so I’d only let them use it when I can supervise or put the phone in a simple child-proof mode, but overall the low cost and no-screen focus are big pluses. D (dedicated audio-only) second: this is the ideal from a routines/screen point of view — no pictures to keep bedtime calmer and a single-purpose device that won’t show notifications or let kids wander into other apps. I’d consider this if the price were reasonable or if someone gave us one, but buying a whole device that costs as much as a low-end tablet makes me hesitate. C (app, audio + images) third: images are nice for a five-year-old who likes pointing at pictures, but using our phone or tablet brings the same worries about other apps, notifications, and screen habits. If the images were optional and the app had a clear kid-lock, I’d be more comfortable, but still prefer audio-first. A (dedicated device, audio + images) fourth: I like the single-purpose idea, but a screen at bedtime is a downside and the price (same as a low-end tablet) makes it hard to justify when an app might do the job. It’s better than an uncontrolled phone app, but for our household I’d probably not buy it unless the cost and return policy were very clear. B (nothing) last: I do value reading aloud and I try to do it when I can, but honestly there are nights I’m too tired or juggling other things, and a reliable audio storyteller could help. I’m wary of handing over devices without checks, so I wouldn’t choose “nothing” by principle — I’d rather try a low-cost, audio-first option and see how it fits us. Practical notes: I’d want a free trial or sample, clear language options (some Spanish phrases would be nice), an easy way to turn off images/notifications, and a simple refund/return policy before committing.

gaz.name: Jorge Luis Castañeda
gaz.justification: My propensity is 3, because I like the idea of a cold, vegetable-forward soup and I’d try it once — but I’m price- and salt-sensitive. If a small ready-to-drink bottle is affordable (say under about $3), tastes fresh, and has a low-sodium, simple-ingredient label, I’d buy it now and then for a quick lunch on a shift. If it’s expensive, overly salty, or tastes like it was made from concentrate, I wouldn’t buy it regularly. So maybe a try, not a definite regular buy.

gaz.name: Darren Paul Schneider
gaz.justification: maybe I would buy it, not sure. I like soups and vegetables, which is a plus, but gazpacho is cold and has a raw, tangy texture that might feel unfamiliar to me. I'd be willing to try a small bottle if it was clearly labeled as mild, the ingredient list looked familiar, and the price was reasonable or it was on sale. I wouldn't buy it regularly unless it tasted more like a mild vegetable soup I already like and wasn't too acidic or spicy.

kids.name: Angela Marie Bautista
kids.justification: She would try the $10 audio-only app first, then the app with images. The dedicated devices cost too much for a single-purpose product, and she prefers audio-only to avoid more screen time. She would not choose no AI stories, but would try them together with her child first.

kids.name: Sarah Beth Lindstrom
kids.justification: E is the easiest and least expensive option to try, and audio-only avoids adding screen time. C is next because illustrations may keep the children interested. B is reasonable if the stories or the app’s handling of requests do not feel right. The dedicated devices cost as much as a low-end phone or tablet for only one use, and A also adds a screen; she would want to test either app with the children first.

gaz.name: Jorge Luis Castañeda
gaz.justification: I’d maybe buy bottled gazpacho. I like vegetables, citrus, and trying foods from other kitchens, but I’d want it to taste fresh and not be too salty. The price and ingredients would matter too.

gaz.name: Darren Paul Schneider
gaz.justification: He said cold blended gazpacho does not sound appealing and that he is very unlikely to buy a bottle.
